title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
summary: Buy once, sell once later, maximise profit. Scan left to right keeping the cheapest price so far; selling today earns `price - minSoFar`. The best of those is the answer.
intuition: The best sell day for today is fixed; the only question is the cheapest earlier buy day.
Keep `minPrice` as you go, so that question is O(1).
If prices only fall, the best profit stays 0 (don't trade).
pitfalls: Selling before buying: the min must come from earlier days only.
Initialising profit to a negative number; the answer is never below 0.
Tracking the global max and min separately ignores their order.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
summary: Grow a window to the right one character at a time. When the new character is already inside the window, jump the left edge just past its previous position. The window always has unique characters, and its widest size is the answer.

complexity.note: Each character is visited once by `r`; `l` only jumps forward.

intuition: `last[c]` remembers the latest index of each character.
If `c` was seen inside the window (`last[c] >= l`), move `l` to `last[c] + 1`.
`l` never moves backward, so use `max(l, last[c] + 1)`.
After fixing `l`, the window `[l, r]` has no repeats; record its length.
pitfalls: Moving `l` back to an old index when the repeat is outside the window ("abba").
Using a set and removing one character at a time works but is two-pointer O(2n); know both.
Off-by-one: the length is `r - l + 1`.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
category: Sliding Window · At most k bad
summary: Find the longest run of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros. Grow the window to the right counting zeros inside it; whenever there are more than k, shrink from the left until there are k again.

complexity.note: Each index enters and leaves the window at most once.

intuition: Reframe: the longest window containing at most k zeros.
Expand `r`; if `nums[r]` is 0, increase `zeros`.
While `zeros > k`, move `l` right, decreasing `zeros` when a 0 leaves.
Every valid window is a candidate answer.
pitfalls: Actually flipping values in the array.
Shrinking with `if` instead of `while` (fine only in the non-shrinking variant).
Forgetting k = 0, where the answer is the longest run of 1s.

title: Fruit Into Baskets
summary: You have two baskets, each holding one fruit type. Find the longest contiguous stretch with at most two distinct types. Count types inside the window with a map; when a third type enters, shrink from the left until one type disappears.

complexity.note: The map never holds more than 3 keys.

intuition: This is "longest subarray with at most 2 distinct values".
Add `fruits[r]` to a count map.
While the map has 3 keys, decrement `fruits[l]` and remove it at 0.
Track the widest valid window.
pitfalls: Forgetting to remove keys whose count drops to 0, so `size()` stays 3.
Restarting from scratch on a third type is O(n²).

Python.code:
def totalFruit(fruits: List[int]) -> int:
    count = defaultdict(int)
    l = best = 0
    for r, f in enumerate(fruits):
        count[f] += 1
        while len(count) > 2:
            count[fruits[l]] -= 1
            if count[fruits[l]] == 0: del count[fruits[l]]
            l += 1
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
summary: You may replace up to k characters to make a run of one letter. A window is fixable when `length - maxCount <= k`, where maxCount is the most common letter inside. Grow right; if the window becomes unfixable, slide it by one.
intuition: Keep the most frequent letter and replace the rest: cost = `window - maxCount`.
When cost exceeds k, move `l` forward one step (the window slides instead of shrinking).
`maxCount` can stay stale-high: the answer only grows when a truly higher count appears.
pitfalls: Recomputing max over 26 counts every step is fine (O(26n)) but not required.
Shrinking with a `while` loop is also correct; just know why the `if` version works.
Counting only uppercase: the problem guarantees 'A'–'Z'.

Python.code:
def characterReplacement(s: str, k: int) -> int:
    count = [0] * 26
    l = max_count = best = 0
    for r, c in enumerate(s):
        count[ord(c) - ord('A')] += 1
        max_count = max(max_count, count[ord(c) - ord('A')])
        if r - l + 1 - max_count > k:
            count[ord(s[l]) - ord('A')] -= 1
            l += 1
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

title: Permutation in String
summary: Does `s2` contain a permutation of `s1`? Slide a window of length |s1| over `s2` and compare letter counts. Keep a `matches` counter of how many of the 26 letters have equal counts, so each slide costs O(1).
intuition: A permutation has the same letter counts, so compare count arrays.
The window has fixed size |s1|: add the new right letter, remove the old left letter.
`matches == 26` means the window is a permutation.
pitfalls: Comparing full 26-entry arrays each slide is O(26n), still fine but slower.
Not handling |s1| > |s2| (answer false).
Updating `matches` incorrectly when a count moves away from equal.

Python.code:
def checkInclusion(s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
    if len(s1) > len(s2): return False
    need, win = [0] * 26, [0] * 26
    for i in range(len(s1)):
        need[ord(s1[i]) - 97] += 1
        win[ord(s2[i]) - 97] += 1
    matches = sum(need[i] == win[i] for i in range(26))
    m = len(s1)
    for r in range(m, len(s2)):
        if matches == 26:
            return True
        i, o = ord(s2[r]) - 97, ord(s2[r - m]) - 97
        win[i] += 1
        if win[i] == need[i]: matches += 1
        elif win[i] == need[i] + 1: matches -= 1
        win[o] -= 1
        if win[o] == need[o]: matches += 1
        elif win[o] == need[o] - 1: matches -= 1
    return matches == 26

title: Minimum Window Substring
summary: Find the smallest substring of `s` containing every character of `t` (with multiplicity). Expand right until the window covers `t`, then shrink from the left as long as it still covers, recording the smallest window seen.

complexity.note: Each pointer moves at most |s| times; the counts use a fixed 128-size array.

intuition: `need[c]` counts how many of each character are still missing.
`missing` is the total still needed; the window covers `t` when it hits 0.
While covered, record the window and move `l` right, putting characters back into `need`.
When a needed character leaves, `missing` goes up and you resume expanding.
pitfalls: Treating `t` as a set; duplicates in `t` must be counted.
Returning the length instead of the substring.
Shrinking with `if` instead of `while`, which leaves windows too big.
